title: AlgoExpert · Number Of Ways To Make Change

slides.heading: Number Of Ways To Make Change
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Dynamic Programming
slides.narration: Let's solve Number Of Ways To Make Change, a medium dynamic programming problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Count combinations of unlimited coins that sum to n.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Count combinations of unlimited coins that sum to n.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Count combinations by processing one coin at a time so order doesn't matter.
slides.narration: Count combinations by processing one coin at a time so order doesn't matter.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Recursion over coins → exponential and double-counts orders
DP with coins in the OUTER loop → counts combinations
slides.narration: Naive recursion is exponential and easily counts the same combination in different orders. Putting coins in the outer loop means each combination is built in a fixed coin order, so it's counted exactly once.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. For each coin, for each amount, add ways of amount minus coin
slides.narration: Step by step. First, ways of zero is one. Second, for each coin, for each amount, add ways of amount minus coin. Third, return ways of n.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: ways[0] = 1 (use no coins)
slides.narration: There's exactly one way to make zero: use no coins.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: After coin 1: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
slides.narration: Adding coin 1: every amount from 1 up gains the ways to make the remainder. With coins one and five, there are 1 ways to make six: six ones, or five plus one.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: After coin 5: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
slides.narration: Adding coin 5: every amount from 5 up gains the ways to make the remainder. With coins one and five, there are 2 ways to make six: six ones, or five plus one.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We set ways of zero to one. For each coin, for each amount from that coin to n, add the ways for amount minus coin. Return ways of n.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n times d. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Loop order matters: amounts outer → counts permutations
slides.narration: If you swap the loops you count permutations instead of combinations, a very common bug.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: Explain the combination versus permutation distinction clearly. A follow-up limits how many of each coin you have.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Count combinations by processing one coin at a time so order doesn't matter.
slides.narration: To recap Number Of Ways To Make Change: Count combinations by processing one coin at a time so order doesn't matter. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
